scope_items.description: EU AI Act high-risk classification and compliance readiness for in-scope AI/ML use cases (e.g. credit-scoring, creditworthiness models)
Model-risk management and governance maturity vs. pace of AI adoption

key_audit_questions.question_text: Which specific AI/ML use cases (e.g. credit scoring, fraud detection, generative AI copilots/chatbots) are in scope for this first AI governance audit, and has GRP completed an EU AI Act risk classification exercise for them?
What is the current status of GRP's AI governance framework relative to DNB's AI supervisory expectations — is this audit testing design only, or also initial operating effectiveness?
Has GRP identified any reliance on third-party foundation models (e.g. OpenAI, Microsoft, Google) for in-scope AI systems, and if so, how is that outsourcing/concentration risk currently governed?
How does GRP currently classify AI systems against EU AI Act risk tiers, and what evidence exists of high-risk system identification (e.g. for credit-scoring models)?
What explainability and bias-testing controls are in place for AI-driven decisioning, and how are they evidenced for supervisory review?
Is there a policy and monitoring control addressing 'shadow AI' — staff use of unsanctioned public generative AI tools with bank/customer data?
What controls exist to detect or mitigate AI-enabled fraud such as deepfake voice/video social engineering against customers or staff?

applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Requires financial institutions deploying or providing high-risk AI systems (e.g. for creditworthiness assessment, fraud detection) to implement a documented risk management system, ensure data quality/governance, maintain technical documentation and logs, provide for human oversight, and ensure accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity. Internal audit must verify compliance of AI model lifecycle controls against these obligations.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: Art. 9 (risk management system), Art. 10 (data and data governance), Art. 11-12 (technical documentation and record-keeping), Art. 14 (human oversight), Art. 15 (accuracy, robustness and cybersecurity) for high-risk AI systems used in credit scoring/creditworthiness assessment

applicable_frameworks.framework_name: EU Artificial Intelligence Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) - Governance & GPAI
applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Mandates that staff deploying AI systems have adequate AI literacy, that deployers of high-risk systems carry out appropriate use, monitoring and incident reporting, and sets transparency/documentation duties on providers of general-purpose AI models (e.g. LLMs) used internally.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: Art. 4 (AI literacy obligations), Art. 26 (obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems), Art. 53 (obligations for general-purpose AI model providers)

applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Requires DNB/ECB-supervised entities to embed AI-based ICT systems within the enterprise ICT risk management framework, including resilience testing, third-party risk assessment for AI vendors/cloud providers, and board-level accountability for ICT (including AI) risk.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: Art. 5-6 (ICT risk management framework), Art. 8 (identification of ICT assets incl. AI-driven systems), Art. 9 (protection and prevention), Art. 28-30 (ICT third-party risk and contractual provisions for AI/cloud vendors)

applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Requires that AI systems making automated decisions affecting customers (e.g. credit scoring) provide for a right to human intervention and explanation, that a DPIA is conducted for high-risk processing, and that personal data used to train/operate AI models is processed lawfully, fairly and proportionately.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: Art. 22 (automated individual decision-making incl. profiling), Art. 35 (Data Protection Impact Assessment), Art. 5(1)(a)-(c) (lawfulness, fairness, transparency, data minimisation)

applicable_frameworks.framework_name: DNB Guidance on Artificial Intelligence / SIRA & General Principles for the Use of AI in the Financial Sector
applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Requires that NL financial institutions supervised by DNB embed sound governance, explainability, fairness/bias testing, accountability, and staff competence requirements for AI applications, and integrate AI-related risks into the institution's systematic integrity and control risk analysis and controlled operational management framework.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: DNB 'General Principles for the Use of AI' (SAFEST framework: Soundness, Accountability, Fairness, Ethics, Skills, Transparency) and SIRA (Systematic Integrity Risk Analysis) requirements under Wft Art. 3:17

applicable_frameworks.framework_name: Wet op het financieel toezicht Art. 3:17
applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Obliges the institution to organise its operations, including IT and model governance for AI, in a controlled and sound manner, with adequate risk management, segregation of duties, and internal control procedures subject to DNB supervision.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: Art. 3:17 Wft - controlled and sound business operations (beheerste en integere bedrijfsvoering), including adequate procedures for risk management of operational processes such as AI-driven decision-making

applicable_frameworks.framework_name: ECB Guide on effective risk data aggregation and risk reporting / SSM supervisory expectations on AI
applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Sets ECB supervisory expectations that significant institutions under direct ECB supervision maintain robust governance, model validation, and data lineage/aggregation controls for AI/ML models feeding into risk reporting, capital calculations, and credit decisions.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: ECB SREP methodology and supervisory expectations on governance of AI/ML models used in risk management, credit decisioning and regulatory reporting (BCBS 239 aligned data aggregation principles)

applicable_frameworks.framework_name: EBA Guidelines on ICT and Security Risk Management (EBA/GL/2019/04)
applicable_frameworks.applicability_rationale: Requires institutions to apply structured ICT risk management, including change management, security testing, and project governance to the development and deployment of AI-based systems integrated into core banking/IT infrastructure.
applicable_frameworks.specific_provision: Section 3.3 (ICT risk management framework), Section 3.4 (information security), covering AI-related IT system change management and project/change management controls

topic_intelligence.topic_primer:
Artificial Intelligence (AI) in internal audit refers to assessing how an organisation governs, develops, procures and uses AI systems (including machine learning and generative AI) to ensure they are safe, compliant, fair and well-controlled.

- **What it means in practice**: Auditing AI covers governance (roles, accountability, policies), model risk management (data quality, validation, bias testing, explainability), lifecycle controls (development, third-party/vendor AI, monitoring, retraining), and specific use cases such as credit scoring, AML transaction monitoring, fraud detection, chatbots and trading algorithms. [Built-in knowledge]
- **Why it matters for a financial organisation**: AI-driven decisions (e.g. lending, pricing, AML alerts) can directly affect customers and create conduct, discrimination, reputational and financial-stability risks; regulators increasingly expect demonstrable human oversight, documentation and risk classification — gaps here are a growing source of supervisory findings. [Built-in knowledge]

background_risk_assessments.section_strategy:
This engagement addresses Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a cross-cutting, Group-wide (GRP) and IT-embedded capability rather than a single business process. AI/ML systems — including credit-scoring and creditworthiness models, fraud detection tools, generative AI copilots and chatbots — are increasingly embedded in core decisioning, customer interaction and IT operations across RET, BUS, AM and INT, making robust governance over their development, deployment and monitoring strategically important to Northwind Financial's safety, soundness and regulatory standing. This is flagged as GRP's first dedicated AI governance audit, meaning there is limited internal audit history to draw on and the review is likely to be a design-and-initial-implementation-adequacy assessment rather than a test of mature, embedded controls.

The main objectives, derived from the regulatory context, are to assess: (1) whether high-risk AI systems (e.g. credit-scoring) have been identified and classified under the EU AI Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/1689) and whether a risk management system, data governance and human oversight arrangements are being built toward compliance; (2) whether model-risk management and AI governance maturity (Wft Art. 3:17, DNB AI guidance, EBA/ECB supervisory expectations) is keeping pace with the speed of AI adoption; (3) whether explainability, fairness and bias controls for AI-driven decisioning meet GDPR and heightened Dutch supervisory/political expectations (post-toeslagenaffaire sensitivity); (4) third-party/foundation-model and outsourcing dependency risk (DORA, cloud/LLM providers); and (5) emerging, less-regulated risks such as AI-enabled deepfake fraud and 'shadow AI' use of public generative tools with bank data.

Prior audits on adjacent topics — though not evidence for this engagement — flag relevant precedent to pressure-test: the 'IT Security Management Review' (in fieldwork) identified an absence of an approved, current information security policy suite at GRP level, which may constrain how AI-related ICT risk is governed; and the 'ESG Risk Framework Assessment' (in planning) repeatedly found unclear governance roles/reporting lines and siloed data governance, a pattern worth testing for recurrence in AI governance given the similarly cross-functional, emergent nature of the topic.
background_risk_assessments.section_risk_tolerance:
Management has not yet articulated a documented risk appetite statement specific to AI; absent an internal framework (flagged as 'not available'), this review should establish whether any Board- or ExCo-approved tolerance exists for AI-related conduct, model, data-protection and operational-resilience risk. Given the regulatory direction of travel — mandatory EU AI Act obligations, DNB's explicit AI/SIRA expectations, and GDPR requirements for automated decisioning — tolerance for non-compliance with binding legal obligations (EU AI Act high-risk obligations, GDPR Art. 22 rights, DORA ICT risk management) should be presumed LOW, consistent with standard supervisory expectations (DNB, ECB/SSM) for regulated financial institutions.

For emerging, not-yet-regulated risks (deepfake-enabled fraud, shadow AI), tolerance is likely to be somewhat higher in a formal compliance sense but should still be considered low from an operational and reputational risk perspective, given heightened Dutch political and NGO sensitivity to AI bias/discrimination in credit decisioning. Residual risk is likely to exceed appetite in areas where no internal AI policy, inventory of high-risk systems, or model governance framework currently exists — this should be a key line of enquiry rather than an assumption, given the 'Internal Framework: Not available' status noted in scope.
background_risk_assessments.section_governance:
Ownership and oversight structure for AI governance at Northwind Financial is not yet documented for this engagement (no internal framework provided) and should be confirmed during fieldwork — specifically, which committee (e.g. Model Risk Committee, Technology/IT Risk Committee, or a dedicated AI governance body) holds accountability, and how this links to existing CRO, CTO/CIO and Board-level reporting lines. The EU AI Act's governance and GPAI provisions place specific obligations on deployers (appropriate use, monitoring, incident reporting, staff AI literacy) and providers of general-purpose AI models (transparency/documentation) — audit should verify these roles have been assigned.

No management information, RCSA results or walkthrough observations specific to AI have been supplied; this is itself an initial observation for a first-of-its-kind audit and should be tested directly (does an AI system inventory exist; is there a risk classification process; is there model validation evidence for AI/ML models feeding risk reporting and credit decisions, per ECB supervisory expectations on risk data aggregation?).

Relevant outstanding issues from adjacent, in-progress engagements should inform fieldwork scoping: the 'IT Security Management Review' finding on the absence of an approved GRP information security policy suite (high residual risk, in fieldwork) may directly affect the control environment AI systems sit within; and the 'ESG Risk Framework Assessment' findings on unclear governance roles/reporting lines and siloed data governance (both in planning) suggest a pattern of governance ambiguity in emergent/cross-cutting risk areas at GRP that this audit should independently test rather than assume.

Compliance measured via: AI system inventory and risk classification, technical file completeness, human oversight evidence, logging/audit trail testing. [HIGH confidence — directly applicable to GRP IT/AI use cases]
- EU Artificial Intelligence Act — Governance & GPAI: requires staff AI literacy, deployer monitoring/incident reporting for high-risk systems, and transparency/documentation duties for GPAI (e.g. LLM) providers. Measured via: training records, incident logs, GPAI vendor documentation review. [HIGH]
- GDPR (Regulation (EU) 2016/679): requires human intervention/explanation rights for automated decisions, DPIAs for high-risk processing, lawful/fair/proportionate data use in training and operating AI models. Measured via: DPIA register, Art. 22 process testing, data lineage review. [HIGH]
- DORA (Regulation (EU) 2022/2554): requires AI-based ICT systems embedded in enterprise ICT risk management, resilience testing, third-party/vendor risk assessment, board accountability. Measured via: ICT risk register coverage of AI, resilience test results, vendor risk assessments for AI/cloud providers. [HIGH]

SUPERVISORY GUIDANCE:
- DNB Guidance on AI / SIRA & General Principles for Use of AI in Financial Sector: requires governance, explainability, fairness/bias testing, accountability, staff competence; integration into SIRA. Measured via: bias-testing evidence, SIRA documentation, explainability artefacts. [HIGH — NL-specific, directly applicable]
- Wet op het financieel toezicht (Wft) Art. 3:17: requires controlled and sound operations, including IT/model governance, segregation of duties, internal controls. Measured via: governance structure mapping, SoD testing. [HIGH]
- ECB Guide on RDA/RRS & SSM supervisory expectations on AI: robust governance, model validation, data lineage for AI/ML feeding risk reporting/capital/credit decisions — relevant if Northwind is a significant institution under direct ECB supervision (TO CONFIRM). Measured via: model validation reports, data lineage documentation. [MEDIUM — applicability depends on supervisory status, to be confirmed]
- EBA/GL/2019/04 (ICT and Security Risk Management): structured ICT risk management incl. change management, security testing, project governance for AI-based systems. Measured via: change management records, security testing evidence. [HIGH]

INTERNAL POLICY:
- No internal AI policy or framework currently available ('Internal Framework: Not available'). This is itself a scope item — audit should confirm existence, approval status and coverage of any internal AI/model governance policy, and escalate as a gap if none exists. [Flagged — not yet assessed]
- EBA Outsourcing GL relevance to third-party/foundation-model dependency (e.g. OpenAI, Microsoft, Google) has not been explicitly confirmed by Topic Intelligence and is flagged as a scope question for the audit team. [LOW/TO CONFIRM]

- Flag confidentiality: AI Act classifications and any gaps discussed today are audit-sensitive, handle per normal IA protocol
- Set collaborative tone — pre-work already done, this meeting is to validate scope and fill gaps, not start from zero
- Confirm timeline expectations up front to avoid surprises later
kickoff_agendas.notes_context:
This audit lands in the 2026 plan because AI adoption is outpacing governance — a classic emerging-risk driver for IA coverage.
- Driver: EU AI Act enters into force with phased obligations; high-risk use cases (credit scoring) carry real compliance deadlines

kickoff_agendas.notes_documentation:

- Control environment expectation: likely immature — AI Act is new, governance frameworks may be in-progress rather than embedded; avoid applying 'steady-state' control testing assumptions

racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "DORA", "source_id": null, "rationale": "No control in the environment specifically addresses identification/classification of ICT assets (AI inventory for DORA purposes, distinct from the EU AI Act use-case inventory control) or protective/preventive ICT security measures and testing; not visible in the passages given.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unverified Art.22 human-intervention process for automated credit decisions
racm_risks.description: Without an assessed/implemented process for human intervention, data subject objection and override of automated credit decisions, customers may be denied an effective remedy against automated decisions, creating regulatory and conduct risk.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "GDPR", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Control 'Verify that GRP provides data subjects with the right to obtain human intervention, express their view and contest automated credit decisions' exists in the RACM, and a related control on human oversight measures for high-risk AI outputs is also listed. However, both are marked design: not assessed, so no evidence of effective implementation (e.g. actual process for data subject requests, documented override mechanism) is available.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: DPIA execution for high-risk AI not evidenced
racm_risks.description: Lack of assessed evidence that DPIAs are actually performed and documented before deployment of high-risk AI (e.g. credit scoring models) could result in non-compliance with Art. 35 and unmitigated privacy risk from AI processing.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "GDPR", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Control 'Verify that GRP conducts a DPIA prior to deploying high-risk AI processing involving personal data' is listed in the RACM but marked design: not assessed \u2014 existence of the control is noted but no evidence of execution, quality, or documentation of completed DPIAs is provided.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Lawfulness and transparency of AI personal data processing not demonstrated
racm_risks.description: Absence of an assessed, GDPR-specific control over lawful basis, fairness and transparency (e.g. privacy notices, purpose limitation) for personal data feeding AI/credit-scoring models creates risk of unlawful or non-transparent processing under Art. 5.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "GDPR", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Partial alignment via the control 'Verify that GRP's data governance process ensures datasets used for high-risk AI meet relevance, representativeness and bias-examination criteria', which speaks to data quality/minimisation concerns, but this is framed around AI Act bias/representativeness requirements rather than GDPR lawfulness/fairness/transparency specifically, and is marked design: not assessed. No control explicitly addresses lawful basis determination or transparency notices for AI processing.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: AI risk not demonstrably integrated into SIRA/controlled operational management
racm_risks.description: Without evidence that AI risk management controls are designed and operating, and without a confirmed link to the SIRA/Wft Art 3:17 integrity risk analysis, the institution cannot demonstrate to DNB that AI risk is systematically identified, assessed and controlled across its lifecycle, risking supervisory findings and unmanaged model risk.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "DNB_SUPERVISION", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Controls describe design intent (not yet assessed) for an AI use-case inventory, a lifecycle risk management system for high-risk AI, and accuracy/robustness/explainability evidencing, but none are confirmed as operating ('design: not assessed'). No named SIRA or Wft Art. 3:17 integration document is visible.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unverified AI literacy and human oversight controls
racm_risks.description: Lack of confirmed, evidenced training programs and effective human oversight/override mechanisms increases the risk that staff cannot adequately supervise, challenge or correct AI system outputs, undermining the Skills and Accountability pillars of DNB's SAFEST framework.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "DNB_SUPERVISION", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Controls reference AI literacy training and human oversight/override measures, but status is 'design: not assessed' with no supporting training records, competency framework, or oversight procedure documentation visible in the passages.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unevidenced bias mitigation and contestability of automated decisions
racm_risks.description: Without confirmed operation of bias-examination in data governance and of a functioning human-intervention/contestability process for automated decisions, the institution risks discriminatory or unfair AI-driven outcomes (e.g. in credit decisioning) and non-compliance with DNB's Fairness, Ethics and Transparency expectations and related data subject rights.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "DNB_SUPERVISION", "source_id": null, "rationale": "A data governance control addressing bias-examination criteria and a control providing data subjects the right to human intervention/contest automated decisions are both listed, but both remain 'design: not assessed' with no bias-testing results, policy, or customer-facing procedure evidenced in passages.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unverified design/operation of AI risk management controls
racm_risks.description: Although controls nominally exist for AI lifecycle risk management, use-case inventory, and human oversight, none have been assessed for design or operating effectiveness and no governing policy document is available. This creates risk that AI-driven decision-making is not actually governed in a controlled and sound manner as required by Art. 3:17 Wft, exposing the institution to supervisory findings from DNB.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "WFT_317", "source_id": null, "rationale": "The control environment lists several relevant controls (AI use case inventory with EU AI Act risk classification, documented risk management system for high-risk AI throughout lifecycle, human oversight measures for override/intervention, AI-driven ICT systems embedded within enterprise ICT risk framework with board-approved policies), but all are marked 'design: not assessed', meaning no evidence has been provided that these controls are actually designed effectively or operating. No policy or charter document has been uploaded to corroborate board-level ownership, documented risk appetite, or escalation lines required for 'beheerste en integere bedrijfsvoering'.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unverified third-party and data governance controls for AI
racm_risks.description: Data governance and vendor risk assessment controls are identified but not evidenced as designed or operating, creating risk that datasets used in high-risk AI systems are not adequately vetted for bias/representativeness and that critical AI/cloud vendor dependencies lack required contractual safeguards, undermining sound business operations under Art. 3:17 Wft.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "WFT_317", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Controls reference data governance for high-risk AI datasets (relevance, representativeness, bias-examination) and third-party risk assessments with contractual provisions for AI/cloud vendors, but these are listed as 'design: not assessed' with no accompanying policy document, procedure description, or evidence of execution.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Absence of evidenced operational safeguards for AI misuse and incidents
racm_risks.description: Without verified controls for staff AI literacy, incident monitoring/reporting, shadow-IT use of public generative AI tools, and AI-enabled fraud (e.g., deepfake social engineering), the institution cannot demonstrate it has adequate procedures to manage the operational risks of AI as required under Art. 3:17 Wft, increasing exposure to undetected misuse, data leakage, and fraud losses.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "WFT_317", "source_id": null, "rationale": "Controls covering AI literacy training, monitoring/incident reporting for AI systems, policy on unsanctioned generative AI tool use, and AI-enabled fraud/deepfake detection are all listed but every one is 'design: not assessed', and no governance document (policy, training record, monitoring log) has been uploaded to substantiate that these controls exist in operation.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Insufficient AI/ML model validation for risk and regulatory reporting models
racm_risks.description: Without a documented, independently validated model risk framework covering accuracy, robustness, and explainability of AI/ML models feeding capital calculations, credit decisions, and regulatory reports, the institution risks regulatory reporting errors, flawed credit decisions, and SREP findings from ECB on inadequate model governance.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "ECB_SSM_GUIDE", "source_id": null, "rationale": "The control environment lists a RACM item 'Verify that GRP's high-risk AI systems achieve and evidence appropriate accuracy, robustness and explainability throughout their lifecycle' and a related risk management system control, but design effectiveness is marked 'not assessed' with no referenced validation methodology, model risk policy, or evidence of independent validation covering models used specifically in credit decisioning/regulatory reporting as ECB expects. No governance documents were uploaded to corroborate implementation.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unverified data lineage and quality controls for risk-reporting AI pipelines
racm_risks.description: Absent documented evidence that data aggregation and lineage controls meet BCBS 239/ECB expectations for AI-driven risk reporting and capital calculation inputs, the bank risks inaccurate or untraceable risk data reaching regulatory reports and senior management, triggering supervisory action.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "ECB_SSM_GUIDE", "source_id": null, "rationale": "RACM control 'Verify that GRP's data governance process ensures datasets used for high-risk AI meet relevance, representativeness and bias-examination criteria' exists as a control objective, but design has not been assessed and no data lineage/aggregation framework document (e.g. BCBS 239 data governance policy) is referenced to confirm it extends to risk reporting and capital aggregation pipelines specifically, as opposed to only high-risk AI Act scope.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unconfirmed human oversight and incident escalation for AI-driven credit/risk decisions
racm_risks.description: Without verified, functioning human-in-the-loop override mechanisms and incident reporting channels for AI models used in credit and risk management, erroneous automated decisions or model failures may go undetected or unescalated, exposing the institution to credit losses, conduct risk, and ECB supervisory criticism of governance.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "ECB_SSM_GUIDE", "source_id": null, "rationale": "RACM includes controls for 'effective human oversight measures enabling intervention in or override of high-risk AI system outputs' and for monitoring operation/reporting serious incidents, but both are marked design 'not assessed', with no board-approved policy, escalation procedure, or incident log evidenced in the passages provided.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Unverified ICT change/resilience governance for AI systems
racm_risks.description: Without an assessed, documented ICT risk management framework covering AI system change control, security testing and resilience testing, AI-driven changes to core banking/IT infrastructure could be deployed without adequate testing or board oversight, increasing operational and security risk.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "EBA_ICT_GUIDELINES", "source_id": null, "rationale": "The control environment references a control intended to verify that GRP has embedded AI-driven ICT systems within its enterprise ICT risk management framework with board-approved policies and resilience testing, but design has not been assessed and no supporting policy or charter document was uploaded to confirm change management, security testing or project governance procedures are actually documented and operating.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Incomplete third-party AI/cloud vendor risk governance
racm_risks.description: Lack of evidenced, operating due-diligence and contractual controls for AI/cloud vendors supporting critical functions could leave the institution exposed to concentration, security and continuity risk from third-party AI providers without appropriate oversight or contractual safeguards.
racm_risks.provenance: {"source_type": "governance_assessor", "source_ref": "EBA_ICT_GUIDELINES", "source_id": null, "rationale": "A control exists to verify third-party risk assessments and contractual provisions for AI/cloud vendors supporting critical functions, but its design has not been assessed and no vendor contract templates, due-diligence procedures, or outsourcing register were provided to confirm operation.", "run_id": "335edb28-0085-4f39-b295-fe58f4b836b3"}

racm_risks.title: Absent AI-specific change and security testing control
racm_risks.description: Without a dedicated control covering structured project/change management and security testing for AI system development and deployment, defects, security vulnerabilities or unauthorized changes in AI models integrated into core systems may go undetected, risking operational disruption or security incidents.

- Media narrative: financial press coverage through 2024-2025 has centred on a 'governance lag' theme - banks racing to deploy generative AI copilots, chatbots and credit/fraud models faster than their model-risk and oversight frameworks can keep up.
- Peer incident: Klarna (Sweden/EU fintech-bank) publicly stated its AI assistant was doing the work of roughly 700 customer-service agents, then partially walked this back in 2024 after acknowledging AI-driven service had degraded quality and re-hiring human staff - now widely cited in Europe as a cautionary tale for AI customer-facing automation in financial services.
- Dutch political attention: the aftermath of the 'toeslagenaffaire' (childcare benefits algorithmic discrimination scandal) continues to drive heightened Dutch parliamentary and public sensitivity to automated/AI-based decision-making in both public bodies and financial institutions, even though that case itself involved the tax authority rather than a bank.

- Civil-society attention: European digital-rights and algorithmic-accountability NGOs (e.g., AlgorithmWatch, Access Now) pushed during EU AI Act negotiations for stronger bias/discrimination safeguards specifically around credit-scoring and creditworthiness AI, which the Act ultimately classifies as high-risk.
